scenes.narration: On October twenty-ninth, the world's biggest crypto exchange lost about six point three billion dollars. Nobody cracked its encryption.
scenes.source: NPR Oct 30 2026; Binance initial report (Nov 3) describes access via employees and the signing service
scenes.imageIdea: dark exchange dashboard, balances glitching red

scenes.narration: Instead, months earlier, an engineer got a friendly message on a real job site. A project director wanted to talk about an exciting new role.

lines: We have a senior role that fits you.
Free for a quick call this week?

scenes.source: Binance initial report via Fortune and SafeDep (Nov 3 2026)
scenes.imageIdea: recruiter DM on a dark job-site UI, generic avatar

scenes.narration: Spread six point three billion over twenty minutes and you get about five million dollars leaving, every single second.
scenes.source: Calc 6.3e9/1200; TRM: most of it moved in ~20 minutes

scenes.narration: So how do you rob a vault guarded by billions in security? You skip the vault, and you go after the people who can open it.
scenes.source: Binance report via Fortune: mainly conventional phishing plus malware

scenes.narration: In this deep dive, we follow every step: one bad download, a fake job, an AI shortcut, and the twenty minutes that emptied the wallets.
Quick favor before we dive in. If you like money and tech explained with real numbers, subscribe and turn on notifications so you don't miss a new video.
Chapter one. Before we get into how it happened, let's understand just how big this theft really is.
According to blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs, the money left Binance wallets on ten different blockchains, and most of it moved in about twenty minutes.
The previous record was the Bybit hack in February twenty twenty-five, at around one and a half billion. This one is roughly four times bigger.
Here's the wild part. Chainalysis says all crypto theft worldwide in twenty twenty-five added up to about three point four billion. This single heist is almost double that.

data.title: ONE HEIST VS A WHOLE YEAR

scenes.narration: Chainalysis tracked about six point seven five billion stolen by North Korea-linked hackers since twenty twenty-two. This one job equals ninety-three percent of that.
So who did it? The FBI says North Korea's TraderTraitor group, the unit also blamed for Bybit. TRM, Elliptic and Chainalysis reached the same conclusion.
scenes.source: NPR Oct 30-31 2026; TechCrunch Oct 30; CNBC Nov 3

scenes.narration: North Korea denies it. Kim Jong Un's sister called the accusation a grave political provocation. So we'll stick to what investigators say: the FBI attributes it to North Korea.

data.claim: North Korea denies involvement in the Binance hack.

scenes.narration: To understand how they pulled it off, you first need to know how an exchange actually guards billions of dollars. That's where the weak spot hides.
Chapter two. An exchange doesn't keep money in one big box. It splits it, mostly to balance two things: safety and speed.
Cold wallets sit offline, slow but very safe. Hot wallets stay online, so customers can withdraw in minutes. This attack hit the hot wallets.
scenes.source: General explainer; Binance says funds left hot wallets (SafeDep, Nov 3)
scenes.imageIdea: two vault panels, right one glowing red

scenes.narration: Why keep so much online at all? Because customers expect withdrawals in minutes, not hours. Every exchange trades a bit of safety for that speed.
On a typical exchange, a withdrawal passes through a chain of checks: your request, risk checks, limits, and finally a system that signs the transaction.
scenes.source: General explainer of typical exchange withdrawal flow

scenes.narration: That last step matters most. Binance has an internal wallet signing service. Whatever it signs, the blockchain treats as a genuine order from Binance.
scenes.source: Binance report via Breach Ledger, mlq.ai (internal wallet signing service)
scenes.imageIdea: central signing node with outgoing beams

scenes.narration: Binance's hot wallets use multi-party computation, or MPC. The key is split into pieces held by different parties, and they must cooperate to sign.
scenes.source: SafeDep (hot wallet uses MPC); general MPC explainer

scenes.narration: That's a strong design. Steal one piece and you get nothing. No single employee, server or laptop holds the whole key.
But here's the clue most people miss. MPC protects the key, not the request. If attackers get the signing system to sign, the math works perfectly for them.
scenes.source: SecurityHQ analysis: protect the transaction path, not just the key
scenes.imageIdea: split panel, request arrow glowing red

scenes.narration: One security firm summed it up: the lesson is to protect the transaction path, not just the key. Keep that phrase in mind for the rest of this video.

data.claim: Protect the transaction path, not just the key.

scenes.narration: So the attackers didn't need the key. They needed three things: a way into a laptop, a way to the right engineers, and permission to run code near the signer.
scenes.source: Analysis based on Binance report sequence
scenes.imageIdea: three tiles lighting up in order

scenes.narration: Step one was finding out who those right engineers were. That started in June, with one search and one wrong click.
scenes.imageIdea: cursor over a glitching search result

scenes.narration: Chapter three. June twenty twenty-six, about four months before the heist. Binance calls the first victim Engineer A.
Engineer A worked on the Wallet DevOps team, the people who keep wallet systems running. He went looking for a popular AI coding tool.
Through a search result, he ended up installing a tampered version of Homebrew, a tool a huge share of Mac developers use to install other software.
scenes.source: Binance report via mlq.ai; Fortune reports an internet ad

scenes.narration: Fortune reports the engineer clicked an internet ad promoting a tampered version, instead of getting the software through Binance's normal channels.

data.claim: The engineer clicked an internet ad promoting a tampered Homebrew.

scenes.imageIdea: news claim card with highlighted phrase

scenes.narration: Think of Homebrew as a toolbox that installs other tools. Poison the toolbox, and anything installed through it can carry the attacker's code.
scenes.imageIdea: toolbox node feeding tool icons, one turning red

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. Binance caught it. Its team saw unusual activity, replaced the laptop and rotated the credentials. Textbook incident response.
But the attackers had already learned Engineer A's role and who else worked on Binance's wallet infrastructure. They walked away with a map.
That's the first clue. Cleaning a device fixes the machine, but it can't take back information that already leaked. Knowledge doesn't get rotated.
And this wasn't a one-off. Binance says it stopped fifty-seven other suspected North Korea-linked attempts in twenty twenty-six alone.
scenes.source: SafeDep summary of Binance report; Fortune Nov 3

scenes.narration: Fifty-seven blocked. It only takes one getting through. Defenders have to be right every time. Attackers only need to be right once.
With that map, the attackers waited. Then, in September, they went after a second engineer, and this time they offered him a job.
Chapter four. Binance calls him Engineer B. His profile on a real job-hunting platform mentioned his experience at Binance. That made him visible.
scenes.imageIdea: glitch title over a profile card

scenes.narration: Someone posing as a project director reached out. Fortune reports the platform was LinkedIn. The pitch looked like a normal, attractive senior role.

lines: We're hiring for our core team.
Can we set up an interview?

scenes.narration: Round one was a video call with an HR representative. Round two was in a chat app, with someone claiming to be CEO of a company that doesn't exist.
scenes.source: SafeDep summary of Binance report; Fortune

scenes.narration: To build trust, the HR representative even shared a personal social media account during the video call. A real face, a real profile, a fake company.

data.claim: An 'HR representative' on a video call shared a personal social media account to build trust.
data.highlight: shared a personal social media account

scenes.imageIdea: claim card, video-call tile beside it

scenes.narration: Every step looked real: a real platform, real conversations, a structured process. That's exactly why this trap works on smart, careful people.
scenes.imageIdea: checklist all green, slightly too perfect

scenes.narration: At the end, the interviewer asked him to download an assignment repository to his work computer. Coding tests are normal in tech hiring. That's the whole point.

lines: Last step: a short take-home task.
Clone the repo and run setup.

scenes.imageIdea: message with a repo link glowing

scenes.narration: The repository ran malicious code during setup. He didn't need to finish the test, or even open the code. Running setup was enough.
scenes.source: SafeDep (repository ran malicious code during setup)

scenes.narration: The malware went after pyenv, a common tool developers use to switch between versions of Python. It sits inside the Homebrew folder.
scenes.imageIdea: pyenv node routing to python versions

scenes.narration: Binance published the exact moves. Create a staging file, write in three thousand four hundred bytes of malicious code, delete the real pyenv, then rename the fake into its place.
scenes.source: SafeDep table of Binance-published file operations
scenes.imageIdea: file log with each line flashing

scenes.narration: Look at the sizes. The real file was three thousand three hundred forty-four bytes. The fake was just seventy bytes bigger. Nobody would notice.
And here's a clue few people know. On Macs, the logged-in user owns the Homebrew folder, so malware can replace tools there without any password prompt.

data.claim: The logged-in user owns /opt/homebrew, so malware can replace tools there without a password prompt.

scenes.imageIdea: folder icon with an open padlock

scenes.narration: The fake pyenv ran commands and connected to an attacker server. Binance says its endpoint security tools did not detect it.
scenes.imageIdea: checklist turning red line by line

scenes.narration: This trick is widespread. In September, agencies from the US, Japan, Australia and Germany warned that one fake-interview group had infected about thirty thousand devices.
scenes.source: Tom's Hardware / IBTimes on WaterPlum advisory (Sep 2026); VERIFY

scenes.narration: One more detail. A Binance spokesperson said employees in non-public roles aren't allowed to keep LinkedIn profiles. The company wouldn't say whether that rule was broken.
Now the attackers were inside a Binance work laptop. But Engineer B didn't hold the keys to the wallets. They needed to move sideways.
Chapter five. October twentieth, nine days before the heist. This is the part that has security researchers most worried.
Using Engineer B's computer and one of Binance's own internal AI tools, the attackers took control of two wallet engineers' machines: Engineer A again, and a new one, Engineer C.
Yes, Engineer A, from June. His old laptop was cleaned, but the attackers already knew he mattered. So they came back for his new one.

data.claim: The attackers took over two wallet engineers' machines, including the one targeted in June.
data.highlight: including the one targeted in June

scenes.narration: On Engineer A's computer they found the prize: a container deployment permission token, a pass that lets you launch software inside company systems.
Why does that matter? A container is a small package of software. With that token, they could start their own code inside Binance's network, close to the signing service.
scenes.source: Binance report via SafeDep (container deployed with Engineer A's token)

scenes.narration: Here's the big unanswered question. Binance hasn't explained how an internal AI tool gave control over other employees' computers. Analysts call it the report's most important gap.

items.text: How did the AI tool grant control?
Why did it have that reach?

scenes.narration: Notice what AI did and didn't do. It didn't break in. Old-school tricks did that. AI was the shortcut once they were already inside.
scenes.source: Fortune: mainly conventional phishing; AI used after access

scenes.narration: Where they stood now: three engineers' machines compromised, a deployment token in hand, and nine days to prepare.
On October twenty-ninth they used everything at once. Let's slow it down and walk through the heist minute by minute.
Chapter six. October twenty-ninth. All times are in UTC. The setup that day started almost three hours before the first coin moved.
Here's the full timeline. Container at seventeen fifteen. Money out at twenty oh five. Last transfer at twenty-three fifty-six. Permission removed at ten past midnight.
At seventeen fifteen, the attacker logged on to Engineer C's computer, used Engineer A's token, deployed a container and ran a malicious script.
That script reached Binance's internal wallet signing service. Remember the lesson: the key was safe, but the path to the signer was now open.
scenes.source: Binance report via Breach Ledger, mlq.ai

scenes.narration: Through the signer, they did two things at once. They sent transfers outside the normal withdrawal process, and they set a trap on Ethereum.
scenes.source: SafeDep (transactions outside normal withdrawal process + 50 EIP-7702 signatures)

scenes.narration: The trap used EIP seven seven oh two, an Ethereum feature added in twenty twenty-five. It lets a normal wallet hand control to a smart contract's code.
scenes.source: EIP-7702 via Ethereum Pectra upgrade (2025; VERIFY date); SafeDep

scenes.narration: But a permission only works if it matches the wallet's next transaction number, called a nonce. So they signed fifty, each with a different number.
Why fifty? A busy exchange wallet keeps sending transactions, so its next number keeps changing. Signing a spread of numbers made sure one would still fit.
scenes.source: Analysis; Breach Ledger describes a 50-nonce spray hitting one live nonce
scenes.imageIdea: number counter ticking while keys fan out

scenes.narration: Think of fifty keys for a lock whose shape changes after every use. Carry every likely shape, and one will fit. One did, and the wallet became a sweeper.

data.claim: One authorization matched the hot wallet's nonce and turned it into a sweeper.

scenes.narration: Security firm SecurityHQ says a single Ethereum transaction carried all fifty authorizations, each pointing the hot wallet at the attacker's sweeper contract.
scenes.imageIdea: transaction inspector, one row lighting green

scenes.narration: About three and a half minutes later, that Ethereum hot wallet was empty, including about one hundred sixty-seven thousand ETH and one point six billion USDT.
Other chains were hit in parallel. Analysts list about two hundred thirty-three million XRP, nearly a million SOL, forty-four million OP, and eighteen thousand bitcoin.
scenes.source: SecurityBoulevard analysis of Binance report; VERIFY amounts

scenes.narration: The XRP part alone left five hot wallets in about four minutes, between twenty oh five and twenty oh nine. This was rehearsed, not improvised.
Binance spotted it and suspended withdrawals. For customers, the app simply stopped letting money out. Inside, a race had started.
scenes.imageIdea: phone with red suspended banner, generic app

scenes.narration: But the off switch didn't reach the blockchain. The delegation lived on-chain, so pausing withdrawals inside Binance couldn't cancel it. Funds kept moving.
scenes.source: SafeDep (delegation stayed active on-chain after withdrawals stopped)

scenes.narration: To cancel it, Binance had to sign a revoke from that wallet. But with MPC, there's no single key to sign quickly. The protection became a speed bump.
scenes.source: SafeDep (MPC: no single private key for fast revocation)

scenes.narration: That's the cruel irony. The split-key design that blocks a lone thief also slowed down the emergency fix.

data.claim: The hot wallet uses MPC, so Binance had no single private key to sign a fast revocation.

scenes.narration: The last unauthorized transfer, about three thousand ETH, left at twenty-three fifty-six. The delegation was cleared at ten past midnight. Nearly four hours of draining.
scenes.source: SafeDep timeline (last transfer 2,961.9 ETH at 23:56; cleared 00:10); calc durations

scenes.narration: Six point three billion was out the door. But stolen crypto isn't spendable money yet. Now the chase began.
Chapter seven. Unlike a bank robbery, every crypto transfer leaves a public trail. So the race started the moment the money left.
Binance says partners froze or intercepted about two point eight five billion. Stablecoin issuers like Tether and Circle can freeze their own tokens, and they did.
scenes.source: SafeDep (citing Binance: $2.85B); Fortune ~$2.5B via Tether & Circle — VERIFY

scenes.narration: Another clue most people miss. Stablecoins look like crypto, but their issuers can freeze them. Bitcoin and ether can't be frozen like that.
The rest is being laundered. Chainalysis tracked more than five hundred million moved through wallets on Tron, then a new phase on Solana.
Elliptic spotted something stranger: they created throwaway meme coins on NEAR and traded them between their own wallets, so stolen coins look like trading profit.
scenes.source: BigGo Finance table citing Elliptic; Mezha

scenes.narration: Keep it in proportion. Four hundred thirty thousand dollars is less than one hundredth of one percent of the haul. This will take a long time.
scenes.imageIdea: tiny sliver on a giant ring

scenes.narration: Chainalysis says North Korea's laundering usually unfolds in stages over roughly forty-five days: fast at first, then slowly blending into the wider crypto world.

data.claim: Laundering typically unfolds in stages over roughly 45 days after a major theft.

scenes.narration: What about customers? Binance reopened withdrawals after about forty-eight hours and says it has replenished ninety-eight percent of the stolen coins from reserves.
Why does North Korea do this? It's cut off from the global financial system, and stolen crypto has become a key source of money.
scenes.source: Chainalysis via The Record and UPI, Dec 2025

scenes.narration: So what should have stopped this, and what can you do so you're never the one who clicks? That's the payoff.
Chapter eight, the payoff. First, let's line up every point where this attack could have been stopped. There were at least six.
A tool from a search result. A test on a work laptop. Undetected malware. An AI tool with too much reach. A token on a laptop. A signer that obeyed.
scenes.source: Analysis based on Binance report (SafeDep, Fortune)
scenes.imageIdea: six items turning red one by one

scenes.narration: Each one has a known fix: run outside code in sandboxes, keep tokens short-lived, limit what AI tools can touch, and require extra approval for unusual signing.
If you work at any tech company, check your own laptop today: no long-lived tokens lying around, no outside code run on work machines, and report odd recruiter messages.
scenes.imageIdea: green checklist on a laptop outline

scenes.narration: Now, you. Meet Maya, a hypothetical twenty-eight-year-old developer. She's job hunting, and she keeps some of her savings in crypto.
scenes.imageIdea: profile tiles, illustrated avatar (not a real person)

scenes.narration: First, the job hunt. Red flags: a company you can't verify, pressure to move fast, and a test that asks you to download and run their code.
scenes.source: Joint advisories on fake-interview campaigns; Binance case details

scenes.narration: Maya's move: before any test, she finds the company's official website herself, and emails a careers address listed there to confirm the recruiter is real.

lines: Hi, is this recruiter on your team?
Confirming before I start the test.

scenes.narration: If she runs a coding test, never on a work laptop, and only inside a disposable virtual machine she can delete afterwards. Remember, setup alone ran the malware.
scenes.source: SafeDep (malware ran during setup; sandbox lesson)

scenes.narration: Second, downloads. Skip sponsored results. Type the official address yourself, or use the link in the project's own documentation. That's exactly what failed in June.
Third, your crypto. Binance customers couldn't withdraw for about forty-eight hours. Imagine Maya needs that money for rent during those two days.
So Maya keeps rent and her emergency fund in a regular bank account. Crypto is only for money she won't need on short notice.
For long-term coins, she could consider self-custody, like a hardware wallet. The trade-off: lose your recovery phrase, and nobody can get your coins back.
If she keeps coins on an exchange, she locks the account down: an authenticator app or passkey instead of text messages, plus a withdrawal allowlist if offered.
scenes.source: General security practice (options vary by exchange)

scenes.narration: And watch for the follow-up scam. After big hacks, fake support agents message people with refund links. Real support never asks for your recovery phrase.

lines: Enter your recovery phrase to verify.

scenes.imageIdea: suspicious DM with red warning overlay

scenes.narration: So, how do you take six point three billion without cracking any encryption? You earn trust, collect access, and get the signer to sign for you.

data.claim: No cracked encryption. Trust, access, and a signer that obeyed.

scenes.source: Binance report via Fortune, SafeDep, SecurityHQ

scenes.narration: Quick recap: a poisoned download in June, a fake job in September, an AI pivot on October twentieth, and the heist on October twenty-ninth.
If you know a developer who's job hunting, or a friend who keeps everything on an exchange, share this video with them. It might save them.
Quick note: this video is for education, not personal financial or security advice. This case is still developing, so check the latest reports.

items.text: Facts may change as reports update

scenes.narration: Fifty-seven attacks were stopped. One got through, and it cost six billion dollars. The weakest link is rarely the code. It's the click.
scenes.imageIdea: final glitch headline, fade to black
